title: Forest Soundscape
description: Immerse yourself in the sounds of the forest and map the acoustic environment.
tasks: Find a comfortable spot in or near a wooded area
Close your eyes for two full minutes and just listen
Identify sounds from three layers: ground level, mid-level, and canopy
Listen for the wind in the leaves — how does it sound different through different trees?
Open your eyes and try to match each sound to its source
observationTips: Forests have distinct sound layers — insects below, birds above
Wind through pine needles sounds different from wind through broad leaves
The best forest soundscapes are heard when there is no wind
natureFacts: Trees communicate through underground fungal networks called mycorrhizae
Old-growth forests can absorb sound, making them some of the quietest places on Earth
The Japanese practice of 'forest bathing' (shinrin-yoku) has measurable health benefits
reflectionQuestion: What sounds disappeared once you started really paying attention?

title: Canopy Observer
description: Look up and explore the world in the tree canopy above you.
tasks: Stand or lie down where you can see the tree canopy clearly
Notice how much sky is visible through the leaves — this is called canopy cover
Count how many different tree species you can see from their leaf shapes
Watch for movement in the canopy — squirrels, birds, or swaying branches
Notice how light filters through the leaves — look for sun spots on the ground
observationTips: The canopy is like a whole separate ecosystem — many creatures never come to the ground
Looking straight up through trees is called a 'canopy view' and is used in forestry
Different seasons dramatically change how much light reaches the forest floor
natureFacts: Forest canopies can reduce temperatures by 5-10°C compared to open areas
Tropical forest canopies contain over half of all species on Earth
Trees in a forest grow taller than isolated trees because they compete for light
reflectionQuestion: When was the last time you really looked up and appreciated the ceiling nature built?

title: Decomposition Detective
description: Investigate the forest floor and the cycle of decay that feeds new life.
tasks: Find a patch of forest floor covered in fallen leaves or needles
Gently move some leaf litter aside — what do you see underneath?
Look for a rotting log — examine its surface for fungi, moss, or tiny insects
Find three stages of decomposition: a fresh fallen leaf, a partially decayed one, and dark soil
Notice the smell — healthy forest soil has a distinctive earthy scent called petrichor
observationTips: The forest floor is one of the most biodiverse zones in any ecosystem
Fungi are the primary decomposers — look for mushrooms and bracket fungi on dead wood
Earthworms, beetles, and millipedes all help break down organic matter
natureFacts: A single teaspoon of forest soil can contain billions of bacteria
The 'earthy' smell of soil is caused by a compound called geosmin, produced by soil bacteria
Dead trees (called 'snags') are vital habitat — over 80 species of birds use them
reflectionQuestion: How does understanding decay change the way you see life?
safetyReminder: Do not touch unknown fungi or mushrooms. Some are toxic. Wash your hands after handling soil.

title: Tree Identification Walk
description: Learn to identify different tree species using leaves, bark, and shape.
tasks: Choose a path with at least five visible trees of different types
For each tree, note: overall shape, bark texture, leaf shape, and any fruits or seeds
Group the trees: needle-leaved (conifers) vs. broad-leaved (deciduous or evergreen)
Find the tallest tree and the widest tree — are they the same species?
Look for any tree that is clearly much older than the others — what makes you think so?
observationTips: Tree shape (silhouette) is one of the fastest identification clues from a distance
Oaks have lobed leaves, maples have pointed lobes, and birches have serrated edges
Seeds and fruits (acorns, samaras, cones) are excellent identification aids
natureFacts: The oldest known individual tree is a bristlecone pine over 5,000 years old
Trees grow from the tips — a carving at eye level on a young tree will be at the same height decades later
Some trees can 'talk' to each other by releasing chemical signals when attacked by insects
reflectionQuestion: How well do you actually know the trees you walk past every day?
